title: Master Class | French, Advance | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky
openingName: French Defense: Advance Variation, Nimzowitsch gambit (4.Nf3), e5-control battle

moves.spoken: The pawn to c5 arrives and the normal move would be c3 — but not here. The knight to f3, leaving d4, is the treatment: an idea of Nimzowitsch's whose whole purpose is to accelerate White's development.
moves.teaches: Nf3 over c3: give the pawn, take the lead in development.

moves.spoken: Develop as if nothing is happening — the bishop to d3, not b5. The bishop to b5 is a very common mistake in these positions: the queenside pin is rarely dangerous, whereas from d3 the bishop points straight at the kingside where Black will castle.
moves.teaches: Prefer Bd3 aiming at the king over the tempting but toothless ...Bb5 pin.

moves.spoken: Now the zen of the whole system: establish total control of the e5-square. That advanced pawn — and the piece that replaces it — is everything. Lose the grip on e5 and Black's pawns start rolling up the board; hold it and Black stays cramped.
moves.teaches: The system lives or dies on control of e5 — a pawn there can be replaced by a piece, but never relinquish the square.

moves.spoken: So the rook comes to e1, reinforcing the e5-point before Black can chip at it. Rook to e1 or bishop to f4 — either adds a guard to the square the whole game revolves around.
moves.teaches: Add defenders to your key square proactively, before it's attacked.

moves.spoken: Recapturing with the knight on e5 keeps the grip — the pawn is gone but a piece takes its place, and control of the square is unbroken.
moves.teaches: A piece can inherit a pawn's outpost; the square matters more than which unit holds it.

moves.spoken: The bishop goes to f4, and don't be seduced by the one-move pin on g5. The goal isn't a cheap pin — it's more control of e5. Even if f4 looks a touch lame, positionally it's the right call because it guards the square.
moves.teaches: Choose the move that serves your strategic goal over a flashy one-move pin.

moves.spoken: Even more control is needed, so combine two jobs in one: develop the last knight to a square where it heads for f3 and adds yet another defender of e5. Bring the undeveloped piece out and let it reinforce the battle square at the same time.
moves.teaches: Develop a piece toward the exact square it can also defend — economy of tempo.
moves.plans: Nd2 then Ndf3, stacking guards on e5.

moves.spoken: With the knight to f3 there are now so many pieces holding e5 that any single one can leave its post and the square still stands — that was the whole point. Just stay alert to the x-ray on the undefended bishop; a later drop back to g3 is the tidy prophylactic.
moves.teaches: Over-guard a square so no single trade or departure loosens it; watch for x-ray discoveries.

moves.spoken: The capture on c6 comes with force — the recapture with the b-pawn is forced, because otherwise the queen simply hangs. That opens the way to collect on d6 next.
moves.teaches: A capture that also attacks the queen forces the recapture — read the in-between threat.

moves.spoken: A textbook never-pre-move moment: the rook takes on c4 looks great, but calculate one move further — Black replies c5 and rips open a massive diagonal for the bishop, and White isn't better. Take the two seconds; the right move is the queen to d4.
moves.teaches: Never pre-move a natural recapture — check one move deeper for the opponent's resource.

moves.spoken: The queen to d4 hits the enemy queen, and a trade there leaves Black's pawn structure in ruins. This is the typical way to convert: force the queens off into a position where the static weaknesses decide.
moves.teaches: Offer a queen trade that leaves the opponent with a wrecked structure.
moves.plans: Qxd4, trade into a better ending.

moves.spoken: The order mattered: taking on e4 first would have let Black grab the dark-squared bishop, so White captured on d6 first and only then won the pawn. Right result, right sequence.
moves.teaches: Sequence captures so the opponent never gets an in-between recapture of a valuable piece.

moves.spoken: And you actually want Black to push the pawn to c4 — the bishop just drops back to e2, and the central chain is no longer under any pressure at all. The advance releases the tension in White's favour.
moves.teaches: Welcome ...c4: it frees the bishop to retreat and de-stresses the centre.

moves.spoken: Objectively the knight to e4 was the inaccuracy — the quiet queen to c7 keeps equality — but even level, White's side is easier to play: healthy improving moves like queen to e2 and rook to d1, full compensation for the pawn, and Black clamped out. The e6-pawn stays a chronic weakness.
moves.teaches: Full compensation plus easy improving moves can make an equal position much easier to play.
